newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian rights campaigner says Chechen poll vital.
newsitem.headline: Russian rights campaigner says Chechen poll vital.

text.p: Russia's leading human rights campaigner said on Wednesday that next Monday's elections in Chechnya would help bring stability to the war-weary region but were not fully democratic because not all refugees could vote.

"All refugees have the right to vote but not all can exercise this right," Sergei Kovalyov, a parliamentary deputy and stern critic of Russia's 21-month military campaign in the breakaway Caucasian region, told a news conference.

An estimated 400,000 people -- nearly half the population -- fled the oil-rich region after President Boris Yeltsin sent in troops and tanks in December 1994 to crush the Chechen rebels' independence bid.

Chechnya's interim government says refugees wishing to vote should return home. Transport will be provided for refugees living in nearby regions like Ingushetia but many live much further afield, in Moscow and other Russian cities.

"The refugees are hardly likely to have the means to fly home to cast their votes," said Kovalyov, who last month called for a postponement of the poll to allow time to prepare voting facilities for all refugees.
"I am convinced that these elections are necessary and will help lead to the stabilisation that Chechnya sorely needs."
Kovalyov said the January 27 elections would lack full legitimacy because of the decision to hold them without arranging for all refugees outside Chechnya to participate.
"The decision is not democratic," he said.
Kovalyov, a dissident in Soviet days, resigned as Yeltsin's human rights commissioner in protest against the campaign, in which tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, died.

Next Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections are a first major step in restoring order in the devastated territory following the signing of a peace accord between the Kremlin and the Chechen rebels last August.
All main presidential candidates regard Chechen independence as a fait accompli, despite a commitment in the peace deal deferring a final decision on political status for five years.
